title: The Div That Couldn’t
subtitle: A clickable div fails four ways.
description: What a real <button> gives you that a div with onClick never will.
prompt:
A card uses `
Save
`. Which set of problems does switching to `
options: Keyboard activation, focusability, screen-reader role, and Enter/Space handling — all free
It adds the text to the page title for SEO
It makes the click handler run faster
Only visual styling improves; behaviour is identical
hints: Try submitting that div with the Tab key only.
What does a screen reader announce for a div?

solution.summary: The correct answer is A — Keyboard activation, focusability, screen-reader role, and Enter/Space handling — all free
solution.answer: Keyboard activation, focusability, screen-reader role, and Enter/Space handling — all free
reasoning: Interactive elements must be reachable and operable by keyboard — a div requires manual tabIndex, role, and keydown handlers.
A button also carries no navigation semantics (unlike <a href>), matching the "perform an action" intent.
Rule: choose the element whose native behaviour matches the interaction, style it afterwards.
whyNot: It adds the text to the page title for SEO — SEO is unrelated to button semantics here.
It makes the click handler run faster — Handler performance is unaffected.
Only visual styling improves; behaviour is identical — The behavioural gaps are exactly the problem; styling is incidental.

learningObjectives: Prefer native semantics over rebuilt behaviour
Name the four free guarantees of <button>
